newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open steady, but seen under pressure.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open steady, but seen under pressure.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries opened mostly unchanged on Friday but are expected to remain under pressure as the market continues to be weighed down by supply, fear of strong data next week and concerns of further rate hikes.
In early trading, the 30-year bond was at 93-26/32, up 1/32 from Thursday, to yield 7.13 percent. The two-year note was unchanged at 99-23/32 to yield 6.53 percent.
As has been the case the whole week, the economic data calendar is light this session, with only existing home sales for March -- due at 1000 EDT/1400 EDT -- slated for release.
Existing home sales are expected to have fallen to a 4.14 million annual unit rate in March, from 4.26 million in February.
Also, the Commerce Department will issue revised trade figures for January and February at 1000 EDT, which comes in the wake of miscalculations found in the initial report.
But the market, players said, is more interested in comments from Federal Reserve officials.
At 1400 EDT/1800 GMT, Richmond Fed President Alfred Broaddus speaks in Virginia, follwed a couple of hours later by Cleveland Fed President Jerry Jordan's speech.

"All these Fed guys have been very consistent -- hawkish and all on the same page," said Marcello Frustaci, senior trader at Daiwa Securities America Inc. "Last year, there were a couple doves, a few hawks and some in-betweens, which is why they didn't tighten. This year they are all talking from the same script.
"That's why we are down here," Frustaci said of a jittery market, noting that the wave of Fed remarks all point to further Fed rate hikes.
The question remains, though, whether the next Fed move will come at the Fed's next meeting in May, or in July.
But Fed concerns are only a part in contributing to the market's poor tone.

Traders also cited supply as a problem. Jim Nealis, managing director of government securities at PaineWebber Inc, noted that about $6 billion in corporate supply was to be issued this week, prompting hedging of Treasuries.
He also said the market is nervous about next week's economic data -- particularly the first quarter employment cost index, due Tuesday. "ECI looms large," he said.
Nealis that expectations for the ECI have worsened as the week went on, which could keep the market from falling much further if reality meets expectations.
Meanwhile, some players expressed fear that the problems with a Japanese insurer could cause selling of Treasuries.
Overnight, Treasuries were range-bound, as light buying in Tokyo was followed by light selling in London.
